claims.text: The proposed material is a tungsten-based matrix containing SRO, identified as strontium ruthenate, precipitates.
The initial W-SRO material contains small, randomly dispersed precipitates.
Controlled annealing can coarsen SRO precipitates in a tungsten matrix.
Controlled annealing can make the SRO precipitate distribution more homogeneous.
Suitable processing conditions include annealing at approximately 1300 °C for 2–10 hours under vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Increasing precipitate size and making precipitate spacing more uniform reduces the effective density of phonon-scattering interfaces.
Larger SRO precipitates decrease phonon boundary scattering in the tungsten matrix.
More uniformly spaced SRO precipitates decrease phonon boundary scattering in the tungsten matrix.
Reduced phonon boundary scattering maintains or improves phonon-driven heat flow through the tungsten matrix.
A coarsened W-SRO composite will have higher thermal conductivity than a compositionally identical baseline containing finer, non-uniform precipitates.
The baseline W-SRO composite contains many fine, randomly distributed precipitates.
Excessively large or numerous precipitates may cause scattering effects to dominate again.
Excessive precipitate size or number may degrade mechanical properties.
The conductivity response may depend on annealing details and precipitate volume fraction.
Precipitate size and distribution can be characterized using SEM or TEM.
Thermal conductivity can be measured by a laser-flash technique.
